newsitem.title: USA: Big B seen falling to buyer.
newsitem.headline: Big B seen falling to buyer.

text.p: Like many other regional drugstore chains, Big B Inc is fighting problems that have accompanied the burgeoning clout of managed health care and huge discount retailers.
The Bessemer, Ala.-based chain has been hurt by deteriorating profit margins and sales, its earnings have disappointed Wall Street and its stock price has languished.
Now the target of an unwelcome bid by Revco D.S. Inc, most experts say the family-owned company has little chance of remaining independent.

"In terms of staying independent, they have to see the handwriting on the wall. Business is going to get a lot tougher before it gets easier for them," said Maurice Levenson of investment advisory firm Value Line Inc.

On Monday, Revco announced it was launching an unsolicited takeover of Big B Inc for $15 per share, or $332 million. Revco disclosed its interest in Big B last month at a meeting between executives of the two companies. Revco followed up with a friendly offer of $14 per share, but Big B said the bid was insufficient.
Big B has said it will consider the $15 per share offer.
Investors, appearing convinced that Big B will be snapped up, have bid its shares up to 16-1/8 this week, up from 12-1/2 before the Revco offer.

People familiar with Big B said top management is not averse to a merger, noting that the company has not enacted a "poison pill" plan to deter a transaction. However, they said management would far prefer to build critical mass through its own acquisitions.
"They are plenty smart to recognize that bigger is better and increasingly important in this business," said Napoleon Overton, analyst at Morgan Keegan & Co.

Big B is an appealing takeover candidate in a period of consolidation that is expected to eliminate many regional chains in the next few years. The consolidation is being driven by pricing pressures imposed by managed health care providers, as well as competition from big discount retail chains such as Wal-Mart Stores Inc.

Although Big B holds the top spot in many of its Southeast markets and is the nation's tenth-largest drugstore chain, its profit margins began tumbling last year, causing it to break a 19-quarter string of improved earnings.
Industry experts said many of the problems stemmed from the company's difficulty in calculating the impact of lower prescription prices paid by managed care providers.
The troubles have persisted and despite record sales, Big B last month saw fiscal second quarter net income tumble to $1.5 million from $3.2 million in the year-ago period.

Although Big B has invested heavily in a new computer system to better track profit margins, people familiar with the company estimate its newly-expanded distribution center is operating at only 60 percent of capacity.
Big B did not return telephone calls.

Big B is dominated by Birmingham's Bruno family, which is estimated to hold about a 20 percent stake of the company. It began operating in 1968 as a unit of supermarket chain Bruno's Inc, but was spun off to shareholders in 1981.
The supermarket chain was sold last year to leveraged buy-out firm Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co for $1.15 billion.
The difficulties have eroded Big B's value as a takeover target in recent months. Analysts last year had estimated the company could be worth $20 per share.

"Management was stretched. I looked at the fact that they had made three or four efforts to expand into different areas of the Southeast only to fail," said John Strauss of investment advisory firm Strauss Financial Group, which sold several hundred thousand shares of Big B about two years ago because he saw little opportunity for earnings growth.
